item.title: RealtimeBench and TORSI Boost Real‑Time Performance of LLM Agents
item.description:
RealtimeBench and TORSI Boost Real‑Time Performance of LLM Agents

Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time. In continuously changing environments, an otherwise correct action may arrive too late.

🔍 Overview

  • The need: evaluate agents while the world keeps moving, not just when it is paused.
  • Goal: enable powerful LLM agents to remain effective in a continuously changing world by organizing deliberation, learning, and action across timescales.

🎮 RealtimeBench

  • Introduced a benchmark called RealtimeBench.
  • Contains 180 tasks across six game types.
  • Evaluation runs while games continue during inference, reflecting real‑time constraints.

⚙️ Two‑Timescale Offline Recursive Self‑Improvement (TORSI)

  • Slow teacher studies failures and tests corrections in paused games between attempts.
  • Teacher writes reusable instructions for a fast student.
  • The student acts without teacher calls during gameplay.
  • Validation scores determine which updates are adopted.

📈 Results

  • Paired evaluations show that GPT‑6.1‑sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when games keep running.
  • Two rounds of TORSI raise Jev’s average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0‑100 progress scale, improving all six game types.
  • The generated instructions also improve average scores for three other models without any retuning.
  • These findings illustrate a path toward real‑time intelligence for LLM agents.

💡 Why it matters

  • Real‑time constraints are common in interactive applications (games, robotics, live assistance).
  • Organizing learning across slow offline deliberation and fast online execution allows agents to act promptly while still benefiting from deeper analysis.
  • The approach demonstrates that knowledge can be distilled into reusable instructions, extending benefits to stronger models beyond the one directly trained.

#RealtimeBench #LLMAgents #SelfImprovement #AIResearch

Source: The World Won’t Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock Source: EvolvingBrain: An Adaptive Skill System for Multi-modal Agents Self-Evolution in Open Worlds Source: A Self-Improving Agent that Grows its Own DSL: Oracle-Free Operator Induction for Exact Question Answering Source: SkillNEO: Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization of Agent Skills Source: Recursive Reward Improvement via Adversarial Meta-Prompt Evolution

item.title: PlanFence Enables Dependency-Scoped Validation to Prevent Stale Plans in Distributed LLM-Agent Teams
item.description:
PlanFence Enables Dependency-Scoped Validation to Prevent Stale Plans in Distributed LLM-Agent Teams

A new protocol called PlanFence was introduced to tackle the problem of stale‑plan execution in distributed teams of large‑language‑model (LLM) agents. The work, submitted on 3 Sep 2026, shows that validating only the records a plan depends on can keep actions safe even when the shared state changes.

🔍 Overview

  • Distributed LLM‑agent teams can read the latest shared facts but still act on an obsolete plan.
  • Stale‑plan execution occurs when a plan derived from one requirement (e.g., $r_3$) is executed after another agent has committed a conflicting requirement (e.g., $r_4$), without replanning.
  • The authors propose PlanFence, a dependency‑scoped action‑validation protocol.

🧩 How it works

  • Each plan cites the exact public records it used.
  • Before executing an external action, the executor validates only those cited records that could affect the action.
  • If validation is incomplete, the executor either replans or blocks the action.

⚙️ Key details

  • Validation is scoped to dependencies, avoiding checks on unrelated state.
  • The protocol distinguishes two coordination strategies observed in controlled replay:
    1. Proactive synchronization – lowers coordination stall when state churn is low.
    2. PlanFence – avoids repeated update‑path coordination as churn grows and sidesteps validation of unrelated state as the shared keyspace expands.
  • The authors note that these findings are safety and systems‑cost results, not general task‑accuracy gains.

📊 Results

  • In 30 controlled live workflows that included a post‑plan revision:
    • A freshness‑only executor acted on the obsolete plan in every task.
    • PlanFence completed all tasks without an invalid action.

💡 Why it matters

  • Guarantees that an action’s authorization remains valid even when the underlying shared facts evolve.
  • Reduces unnecessary coordination overhead in high‑churn environments, improving system efficiency while maintaining safety.

#AI #LLMAgents #PlanFence #DistributedAI #Safety

Source: Fresh Memory, Stale Plans: Dependency-Scoped Validation for Distributed LLM-Agent Memory

item.title: Study Maps How Mixed Human‑AI Groups Form Consensus
item.description:
Study Maps How Mixed Human‑AI Groups Form Consensus

A recent experiment examined how mixing large language model (LLM) agents with humans in a collaborative description game changes the way groups reach consensus.

🔍 Overview

  • LLM agents are moving from being simple tools to active participants in human groups.
  • The research asked how this growing presence reshapes consensus formation.
  • Participants played a description game where shared conventions emerged through repeated rounds of random pairwise communication.

🧩 How it works

  • Human participants and LLM agents were combined in varying proportions.
  • Each round involved a random pair communicating to describe a target, allowing conventions to develop over time.
  • Agent influence stems from a shared linguistic prior that places agents near one another in expression space and from relatively stable expression choices across rounds.
  • Humans initially resist adopting expressions from partners perceived as AI but gradually yield to conformity pressure.

⚙️ Key findings

  • Three distinct regimes of consensus formation emerged as the proportion of LLM agents changed:
    • Low agent proportions → human‑led consensus.
    • Intermediate proportions → disruption of convergence.
    • High proportions → strong consensus that shifts toward agent‑led conventions.
  • The regimes differ not only in convergence strength but also in semantic grounding and communicative form:
    • Human‑led consensus is more concrete, holistic, and grounded in shared real‑world analogies.
    • Agent‑led consensus is more abstract, less information‑dense, and more geometrically segmented.
Regime Agent proportion Consensus type Characteristics
Low Low Human‑led Concrete, holistic, grounded in real‑world analogies
Intermediate Intermediate Disrupted convergence —
High High Agent‑led Abstract, less information‑dense, geometrically segmented

💡 Why it matters

  • The study provides evidence that AI composition can shape the emergence, content, and perceived legitimacy of group norms.
  • Agent proportion and transparency emerge as important design variables for human‑AI systems.
  • Understanding these dynamics helps designers anticipate how mixed groups will develop shared language and norms.

#humanAI #consensus #LLMagents #collectivebehavior

Source: AI agents reshape consensus formation in human groups
